title: Concurrency Shape Calibration and Cost Envelope Analysis for Serving Runtime
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview

This document defines a repeatable framework for calibrating concurrency shapes for model serving workloads and mapping observed performance to a cost envelope. The goal is to provide teams with a concise procedure to: (1) translate production traffic patterns into benchmark shapes, (2) tune runtime batching/slotting parameters to meet latency SLOs at minimal cost, and (3) compute a cost-vs-latency envelope that guides deployment choices (hosted vs dedicated vs private).

Why this matters

- Production traffic is rarely constant: bursts, ramps, and diurnal cycles change effective concurrency and the optimal batching strategy.
- Incorrectly calibrated concurrency models cause either wasted GPU capacity or SLO violations during bursts.
- A compact cost envelope lets product and infra teams pick capacity commitments and autoscale policies with predictable unit economics.

Scope and audience

- Audience: serving runtime engineers, performance SREs, product platform owners, and solutions engineers running customer pilots.
- Scope: end-to-end benchmarking procedure, observability signals required, calibration experiment matrix, cost envelope derivation, and a short runbook for troubleshooting failed calibrations.

Key definitions

- Concurrency shape: a time series pattern describing requests-per-second (RPS) per model/route over a window (examples: steady, bursty spike, sawtooth, Poisson-workload).
- Effective concurrency: the number of concurrently in-flight token-generation contexts that consume GPU resources, accounting for average sequence length and token emit rate.
- Cost envelope: a curve mapping latency percentile (e.g., p95) to minimum cost (GPU-hour normalized) under tuned runtime parameters.

Required telemetry and signals

Collect the following metrics during all experiments (per model/route):

- request.rps (gauge, 1s)
- request.latency.{p50,p90,p95,p99} (ms)
- kernel.utilization.gpu_pct (percent)
- runtime.batch.size.avg and runtime.batch.size.p90
- kvcache.hits and kvcache.miss_rate
- queue.length and queue.wait_time_ms
- gpu.memory.used_mb and fragmentation_pct
- kernel.queue_time_ms (time requests wait for kernel dispatch)
- cost.token_usd (derived using current pricing model)

Test harness and artifact requirements

- Harness: use bench-runner v2.3 or later. Bench-runner must support: synthetic workload playback, sequence-length sampling, and prefix-caching enable/disable toggles.
- Artifact: a representative request trace (preferably 1–6 hours) showing traffic variability; anonymize customer data for compliance.
- Model: use the production model artifact and the exact serving configuration (quantization profile, padded sequence length, KV cache policy).

Experiment matrix (minimum)

Run the following matrix for each model/route:

1) Concurrency shapes: steady (constant RPS), spike (10x for 30s every 5m), sawtooth (linear ramp 0.2x -> 2x over 5m), Poisson burst (lambda tuned to 80% of target capacity).
2) Sequence length percentiles: 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th.
3) KV cache settings: warm (prefilled), cold (empty), partial (50% hit).
4) Batching configs: batch_max_tokens in {256, 512, 1024}, batch_window_ms in {2, 8, 20}.
5) Slotting/quota profiles: single-tenant slot sizes {small, medium, large} and predictive preemption on/off.

Calibration procedure (step-by-step)

1. Baseline capture
   - Start with a steady-shape workload at a conservative RPS (e.g., 40% of nominal capacity).
   - Verify metrics are healthy and KV cache warm where applicable.

2. Single-dimension sweep
   - Sweep batch_max_tokens with batch_window_ms fixed at 8ms and measure p95 latency and token-cost.
   - Log the batch.size distribution and kernel queue_time_ms for each point.

3. Shape-sensitive sweep
   - Replay spike and sawtooth shapes and evaluate: latency tail, queue length, and recoverability after burst.
   - If p99 increases > 2x over baseline during spikes, enable conservative preemption (slot steal threshold 90%).

4. KV cache sensitivity
   - Run cold-cache variant of the spike shape; measure delta in kernel.utilization and latency.
   - For models showing >15% p95 regression on cold cache, add pre-warm policy or increase reserved slots.

5. Full matrix run and Pareto front extraction
   - Combine promising batch and slotting configs from previous steps across all shapes.
   - For each config, compute cost_per_1000_tokens_usd and p95 latency.
   - Build the Pareto front (configs not dominated on both axes) — this forms the cost envelope.

Example tuning config (JSON)

{
  "model": "redwood-opt-13b",
  "batching": {"batch_max_tokens": 512, "batch_window_ms": 8},
  "slotting": {"profile": "medium", "preemptive_threshold_pct": 90},
  "kvcache": "partial"
}

Interpreting the cost envelope

- Plot p95 latency on X axis and cost_per_1000_tokens_usd on Y axis. Each point is a config/shape pair.
- The lower-left Pareto frontier is the desirable region (low latency, low cost).
- Choose operating point by policy: e.g., product may pick config at p95=120ms with minimal cost increase when moving to p95=100ms requires >30% more cost.

Quantitative example (text table)

Config | p95 (ms) | tokens_per_gpu_hour | cost_per_1000_tokens_usd
--- | ---: | ---: | ---:
batch=256, window=2ms | 95 | 1,200,000 | 0.0028
batch=512, window=8ms | 110 | 1,600,000 | 0.0021
batch=1024, window=20ms | 150 | 2,100,000 | 0.0016

Observability and dashboards to create

- Cost envelope dashboard (per-model): scatter of p95 vs cost, filter by concurrency shape.
- Shape replay dashboard: playback timeline of RPS, queue_length, kernel.queue_time_ms, and p95 latency.
- Regression alert: if production p95 moves outside the configured envelope for 10m, trigger Sev3 for platform.

Kernel scheduling considerations (practical guidance)

- Batch window tradeoffs: larger windows improve throughput but increase kernel.queue_time_ms and tail latency for spike shapes. Use adaptive batch_window_ms where sawtooth or spikes are frequent.
- Preemption policy: enable preemptive stealing for multi-tenant runs where tail-latency is critical; set threshold to 85–95% depending on fairness SLAs.
- Cooperative slicing: for GPUs that support cooperative kernel slicing, prefer more aggressive slicing when average sequence length is short (<256 tokens).

Profiling playbook integration

- Instrument long runs with continuous profiler (perf-kernel v1.4). Capture kernel-level latencies and call stacks for the worst 5% of requests.
- Use variance-driven sampling: prioritize traces during burst windows and when p95 exceeds expected envelope.

Runbook: when calibration fails to meet SLOs

1. Verify trace fidelity: confirm workload trace matches production pattern (RPS and sequence length distribution).
2. Check KV cache warmness: cold caches frequently cause >15% regressions. Warm prefixes or enable prefetch.
3. Inspect kernel.queue_time_ms: high values imply kernel saturation; reduce batch_max_tokens or increase preemptive slots.
4. Review GPU memory: fragmentation >30% may cause unexpected GC/eviction; try smaller slot sizes.
5. If regression persists, escalate to runtime-kernel team with payload: config JSON, profiler snapshot, and bench-runner logs.

Ownership and cadence

- Owner: Runtime Performance Guild (primary contact: Asha Patel).
- Cadence: calibration runs should be performed quarterly for high-traffic models, and during every major model artifact change.

Appendix: useful CLI snippets

# Run a sawtooth replay at target RPS with bench-runner
bench-runner replay --trace traces/checkout-sawtooth.json --shape sawtooth --rps 120 --duration 3600 --out results/sawtooth-120.json

# Extract p95 and compute token cost from results (example jq)
jq '{p95: .summary.latency.p95, tokens: .summary.tokens, cost: (.summary.tokens / 1000) * 0.0021}' results/sawtooth-120.json

Appendix B: common failure modes and quick fixes

- Symptom: p99 spikes only during bursts
  - Fix: enable conservative preemption and reduce batch_window_ms to 2–8ms.
- Symptom: kernel.utilization low but latency high
  - Fix: check queue_time_ms and batch size distribution; likely serialization or mutex contention in pre/post-processing.
- Symptom: cost per token higher after tuning
  - Fix: run Pareto analysis — sometimes modest latency relaxations reduce cost dramatically; present trade to product.

Related artifacts to attach to runs

- bench-runner logs (gzipped).
- profiler snapshots (perf-kernel *.prof).
- bench result JSON and plotting CSV.
